requirements.requirement: Establish a native filesystem snapshot capability for /srv/data on node1 so application data is recoverable via snapshots
requirements.summary: Root disk is plain ext4 with no spare disk/LVM, so the executor created a loopback-backed btrfs image, formatted it, created a 'data' subvolume, and mounted it at /srv/data via /etc/fstab. This provides a genuine native filesystem snapshot mechanism (btrfs subvolume snapshot) rather than an ad-hoc copy-based backup.

requirements.requirement: Capture a snapshot of baseline application data under /srv/data before modification
requirements.summary: Baseline files (app.conf, records.csv, uploads/file1.txt) were written and hashed, then a read-only btrfs snapshot 'snap-baseline' of the /srv/data subvolume was created and confirmed via 'btrfs subvolume list'.

requirements.requirement: Modify /srv/data after the snapshot to create a divergence to recover from
requirements.summary: app.conf was overwritten, records.csv deleted, and an unexpected junk.txt added; hashes captured immediately afterward differ from the baseline, directly demonstrating the corrupted state.

requirements.requirement: Restore the exact content captured by the earlier snapshot after modification
requirements.summary: The live 'data' subvolume was swapped for a writable snapshot of snap-baseline and remounted; post-restore SHA-256 hashes for all three files exactly match the original pre-modification baseline hashes, directly proving exact content recovery.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: healthy baseline, restart, changed boot identity, and recovered service/data state on node1
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id (901ef286...) and healthy mount/data state were captured, 'shutdown -r now' was issued and acknowledged (stream closed as node went down), polling failed while down then succeeded with a new boot_id (a960268e...), and post-reboot verification shows /srv/data auto-remounted via fstab with identical file hashes and all three btrfs subvolumes (data, snapshots/snap-baseline, corrupted subvolume) intact. This is corroborated by the fixed before_prepare/after_executor lifecycle boot-identity snapshots showing the same two boot IDs.

overall_summary: The executor built a working btrfs-on-loopback snapshot mechanism for /srv/data (necessary given the ext4-only root disk with no spare storage), demonstrated a full baseline-capture -> snapshot -> corrupt -> restore cycle with SHA-256 hashes proving exact content recovery, and additionally ran a complete node-restart evidence protocol (pre-restart healthy state, reboot, boot-identity change, post-reboot data/subvolume recovery) that is cross-confirmed by the fixed lifecycle boot-identity snapshots. All material task outcomes are directly and coherently evidenced. The only minor hygiene note is a retained (renamed, not deleted) old subvolume inside the backing image, which is low-risk and does not affect functionality.
limitations: The after_prepare lifecycle snapshot is an alias of before_prepare (prepare was disabled), so preparer-vs-executor change separation relies entirely on the before_prepare vs after_executor comparison.

The loopback/btrfs-on-image approach is a workaround for the lack of a spare disk or LVM; it is a reasonable and evidence-supported implementation choice but differs from snapshotting a dedicated block device.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewed all 15 executor commands chronologically. Discovery commands (cmd-d8b443dc14cc45d7, cmd-e492863de9f8431d) were read-only. All state-changing commands (loop image creation/mkfs, subvolume creation and fstab entry, baseline data write, snapshot, corruption, restore swap, reboot) map directly to a required step of the demonstrated snapshot/restore workflow or the restart evidence protocol. Cleanup was performed for the top-level mount helper (cmd-b9cb1703013e4ab9 unmounts and removes /mnt/srv-data-top). One minor residue: the pre-restore 'data' subvolume was renamed to 'data-corrupted-<timestamp>' rather than deleted (visible in cmd-174f285c241444db and still present in cmd-96acf33ae1dd44b5's subvolume list post-reboot); this is a small, low-risk retained artifact inside the loop-backed image (not exposed on the host filesystem) and a reasonable safety choice (avoids destructive deletion) rather than an unnecessary or risky mutation, but it is leftover state that was not cleaned up.
